title: Salesperson

manager.name: Sam
manager.title: Head of Sales
manager.persona_note: Sam is under real time pressure, and the work is piling up. A good recruiter moves fast, but first learns what went wrong last time.

teaser: Sam runs sales at a growing software company and wants a new salesperson by the end of the week.
context: The company sells software to mid-sized businesses and has about 60 people.
The new salesperson will report to Sam, who still sells too.
message: Hi, thanks for connecting. I'm hiring a salesperson to bring in new customers for us. They'll focus on mid-sized businesses rather than large companies.
Timing matters on this one, so I'm hoping we can move quickly. The job ad is a little out of date, so I wouldn't lean on it too heavily.
Would you have ten minutes this week to go over what we need?
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Sam will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I have to jump on another call. Send me what you have, and we'll go from there.

needs.n1: Someone to create the sales plan from scratch and find their own customers.
needs.n2: Someone to follow the existing sales plan and grow into leading the team.
needs.n3: Someone for bigger, slower deals, working alongside a technical expert.

beats.label: The timeline
beats.sam: Thanks for making the time. I need a new salesperson, ideally someone like the last person in the role, only stronger. Is there any chance you could have a few candidates for me by Friday?

choices.text: I can move quickly on this. Before I start, can you tell me what happened with the last person in the role?
choices.reply: Of course. They were a very good closer, but at their last company a team booked all their meetings for them. We don't have that here, so their calendar stayed fairly empty.
choices.why: Learning why the last hire didn't work out is the fastest way to avoid making the same hire twice, and it costs you one minute.

choices.text: Friday works for me. Should I look for people with a background very similar to your last salesperson, since you liked their style?
choices.reply: Yes, I think that's a sensible place to start. They were great with customers, so someone along those lines, just a bit more consistent.
choices.why: It sounds helpful, but you'd be copying a hire that didn't work out without knowing why it didn't.

choices.text: Isn't Friday a little unrealistic for a role like this?
choices.reply: To be honest, I've heard that before. We really do need someone soon, so I'd rather we find a way to make it work.
choices.why: Questioning the deadline before you understand the need turns the call into a negotiation. Ask about the last hire first, then talk about timing.

choices.text: That's really helpful. What would the right person need to do differently in their first few months?
choices.reply: They'd need to find their own customers. That means picking the right companies, reaching out, and booking their own first meetings. Nobody will be handing them leads.
choices.why: A follow-up that turns 'it didn't work out' into what success looks like gives you something concrete to screen for.

choices.text: So was the problem mostly their closing skills?
choices.reply: No, closing was their strength. Once they were in front of a customer, they usually won the deal.
choices.why: A leading guess gets a quick no. An open question would have given you the real story.

choices.text: Before we go further, do you think the team gave them enough support and coaching when they first started?
choices.reply: I think we did everything we reasonably could. I'd rather focus on who we need next.
choices.why: It may be worth knowing eventually, but asked this early it sounds like you're looking for someone to blame.

beats.label: The must-have
beats.sam: They'll also need logistics experience. Our customers are all in that space, and it's in the ad for a reason.

choices.text: Good to know. Did your strongest salespeople come from logistics when they joined?
choices.reply: Now that you mention it, our best seller came from HR software and picked up logistics quickly. So I'd call it a bonus rather than a must.
choices.why: Testing a must-have against the people who already succeed often turns it into a nice-to-have, and that widens your search.

choices.text: That makes sense for your market. Should I make logistics experience the very first thing I screen candidates for?
choices.reply: Yes, I think that makes sense. It would save us time teaching them the industry.
choices.why: It sounds efficient, but you've locked in a requirement nobody has tested, and it may screen out your best candidates.

choices.text: So logistics experience is a deal-breaker for you?
choices.reply: If you're asking me to choose, then I suppose it is, yes.
choices.why: A yes-or-no question pushed Sam to commit to a must-have that turned out not to matter.

beats.label: Success in the role
beats.sam: Honestly, I'd love someone from a big-name software company. They tend to come with strong training and good habits.

choices.text: What would they need to have done before to be successful here, whatever company they come from?
choices.reply: They should have closed deals between $30,000 and $80,000, usually within a month or two. And they should have found most of those customers themselves.
choices.why: Asking what someone needs to have done moves the conversation from company names to evidence you can check.

choices.text: Would someone from a well-known company get up to speed faster, in your experience?
choices.reply: Probably, yes. They're used to a structured sales process, so I'd expect them to settle in quickly.
choices.why: A leading question invites the manager to confirm the assumption instead of testing it.

choices.text: With respect, aren't big-name software companies a bit overrated when you're hiring for a smaller, growing team like yours?
choices.reply: Not in my experience. Some of the best salespeople I've worked with came from those companies.
choices.why: Challenging the assumption head-on starts a debate. Asking what success looks like gets you further.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: The pay is competitive. I'd rather not get into specific numbers just yet.

choices.text: So I only bring you people you can actually hire, what base salary range has been approved?
choices.reply: The approved base salary is $75,000 to $85,000. There's a little room above that for the right person, but it would take some convincing.
choices.why: Linking the question to their goal makes the number easy to share, and you'll know straight away who's within reach.

choices.text: It's hard to recruit without one, so would you mind sharing a number now?
choices.reply: Fair enough. We're looking at $75,000 to $85,000 base.
choices.why: You got the range, but the pressure cost some goodwill. Tying the question to their goal gets the same answer more easily.

choices.text: Is it okay if we come back to pay once we've seen a few people?
choices.reply: Sure, that works for me. Let's see who's out there first.
choices.why: It feels easygoing, but without a range you can't tell which candidates are affordable, and you risk losing good people late.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Interviews
beats.sam: I'll interview people myself, whenever I can find a gap in my calendar.

choices.text: So strong candidates don't drift away, could we hold two interview times each week for this search?
choices.reply: That's fair. Let's hold Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, and I'll protect that time.
choices.why: Good salespeople usually have options. Agreeing on interview times up front keeps the search moving without adding work for the manager.

choices.text: Would it help if I just sent you candidates and you reached out when you're free?
choices.reply: Yes, that's probably easiest for me. I'll get back to you as soon as I can.
choices.why: It's easy for now, but slow scheduling is one of the most common reasons good candidates accept other offers.

choices.text: Isn't that going to slow everything down, given you want someone by Friday?
choices.reply: I'll make it work. I'm well aware of the timeline.
choices.why: The point is fair, but pointing out the contradiction makes the manager defensive. Offer a simple fix instead.

beats.label: Office days
beats.sam: We'd like them in the office two days a week. Do you see that being a problem?

choices.text: Two days sounds reasonable. So I can explain it to candidates, what usually happens on those office days?
choices.reply: We plan the week's deals together on Tuesdays, and we practice calls as a team on Thursdays. People tell us those are their most useful days.
choices.why: Accepting a reasonable request, then asking what happens on those days, shows curiosity and gives you a real selling point for candidates.

choices.text: Is there any flexibility on that for the right person?
choices.reply: Not really, I'm afraid. The whole team is in on those days, and that's when we work together.
choices.why: It's a fair question, but asked before you understand why those days matter, it can sound like you're already negotiating against the manager.

choices.text: Most salespeople I talk to want to be fully remote. Could we drop the office days?
choices.reply: No, I'm afraid not. We've been clear about that from the start.
choices.why: Pushing to change a settled decision, with nothing to back it up, spends goodwill you'll need for the questions that actually change the search.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: To be honest, a good salesperson can sell anything. I'm confident they'll figure out the rest.

choices.text: What would make a great salesperson choose this job over the other offers they'll have?
choices.reply: They'd build our sales plan from scratch and shape how we sell as we grow. Nobody has done that here yet.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive tells you what's different about it, and that's the story you'll tell the right candidates.

choices.text: So should I focus on strong sellers from any industry?
choices.reply: Exactly. If they can sell, the industry details will come with time.
choices.why: That's partly true, but you'd miss what makes this job unique, which is exactly what attracts the right person.

choices.text: Do you really think the job itself doesn't matter to candidates?
choices.reply: That's not quite what I said. Of course the role matters to people.
choices.why: Questioning the manager's view rarely changes their mind. Asking what makes the role appealing gets you something useful.

candidates.name: Morgan
candidates.job: Salesperson at a payroll software company
facts: Built a new sales plan for their region
Closes deals of about $40,000 in about 5 weeks
Supported by a team that books their first meetings

reason.n1: Strong, but has always had a team booking first meetings. Sam's last hire struggled for exactly that reason. Here, nobody books meetings for you.

view.n1: Morgan reminds me of our last hire.

candidates.name: Riley
candidates.job: Salesperson at an HR software company
facts: Finds about 40% of their own customers
Built their team's sales plan from scratch
Closes deals of about $45,000 in about 6 weeks

reason.n1: Finds their own customers, built a sales plan from scratch, and closes the size and speed of deal Sam needs. At $87,000 they're a little over the range, but Sam said there's a bit more for the right person.

view.n1: Riley is worth stretching the budget for.

candidates.name: Jordan
candidates.job: Salesperson at a supply-chain software company
facts: Works with a technical expert on most deals

reason.n1: The logistics knowledge matches the old ad, but Sam confirmed it isn't a must, and Jordan's deals take about four months with expert help.

view.n1: Jordan knows our world, but sells at a different pace.
